Q1.text: Neural IR models had often been studied in homogeneous, narrow settings, limiting insight into their out-of-distribution generalization.
It was unclear how well trained neural retrieval models perform on other text domains or retrieval tasks, and how different approach types (sparse vs dense) generalize out of distribution.

Q2.text: Prior work commonly trains and evaluates neural retrievers on the same large dataset (e.g. NQ, MS MARCO), which does not reveal how they perform elsewhere.
Building large training corpora is time-consuming and expensive, so many retrieval systems are deployed zero-shot with no target-domain training data.

Q3.text: Existing retrieval benchmarks such as MultiReQA and KILT were narrower: they focused on a single task, small corpora or a certain domain, and did not evaluate zero-shot retrieval in depth.
MultiReQA covers only question answering, is mostly Wikipedia-based (5 of 8 datasets), and 6 of 8 tasks have fewer than 100k candidate sentences.
KILT covers five knowledge-intensive tasks (eleven datasets) but retrieves only from Wikipedia and treats retrieval as a secondary component rather than the primary task.

Q4.text: The authors built BEIR, a benchmark of 18 zero-shot retrieval datasets spanning 9 heterogeneous tasks and domains.
They released an open-source Python package (installable via pip) that converts datasets into a standardized corpus/queries/qrels format and wraps multiple retrieval libraries for evaluation.
They evaluated ten retrieval systems spanning five architecture families (lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction, re-ranking) on the benchmark.
They ran a bias study, manually annotating 980 missing query-document pairs in TREC-COVID to measure the impact of lexical annotation bias.

Q5.text: Datasets were selected using four criteria: diverse tasks, diverse domains, sufficient task difficulty, and diverse annotation strategies.

nDCG@10 was chosen as the single primary metric: Precision and Recall are rank-unaware, and binary rank-aware metrics (MRR, MAP) cannot evaluate graded relevance judgements, whereas nDCG suits both binary and graded relevance.
Documents were truncated to the first 512 word pieces for all neural models due to transformer input-length limits.

Q6.text: A zero-shot comparison of 10 models across 18 datasets plus in-domain MS MARCO, reporting nDCG@10 for each model-dataset pair.
A latency and index-size study on a randomly sampled 1-million-document subset of DBPedia, measured on both CPU and GPU.
A manual re-annotation study on TREC-COVID measuring Hole@10 and nDCG@10 before and after adding missing relevance judgements.
An ablation comparing two otherwise identically trained DistilBERT dense models using cosine similarity vs. dot product, on TREC-COVID, Signal-1M(RT) and FEVER.

Q7.text: The re-ranking model BM25+CE had the best average zero-shot performance relative to BM25 (+11%) and outperformed BM25 on 16 of 18 datasets, failing only on ArguAna and Touché-2020.
The late-interaction model ColBERT averaged +2.5% relative to BM25 and outperformed BM25 on 9 of 18 datasets.
The document-expansion model docT5query averaged +1.6% relative to BM25 and outperformed BM25 on 11 of 18 datasets.
DPR, the only dense model not trained on MS MARCO, generalized worst, averaging -47.7% relative to BM25.
The term-weighting sparse models underperformed BM25 on average: DeepCT -27.9% and SPARTA -20.3%.

Q8.text: In-domain performance on MS MARCO does not predict a model's zero-shot generalization across BEIR: BM25 trails neural models by 7-18 points in-domain yet is a strong zero-shot baseline.

There is a trade-off between generalization and computational cost: the best-generalizing re-ranking and late-interaction models are the slowest (>350ms per query), while dense retrievers are 20-30x faster (<20ms).

After the missing TREC-COVID judgements were filled in, lexical systems barely changed (docT5query 0.713 to 0.714), while the dense retriever ANCE rose from 0.654 to 0.735, moving from slightly below BM25 to 6.7 points above it.

BEIR datasets can carry a lexical annotation bias, likely because lexical retrieval systems were used to build annotation candidate pools, which disadvantages non-lexical models. Even TREC-COVID's multi-system pool remained biased toward lexical approaches.

Q9.text: The benchmark covers English-only datasets; multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval were not evaluated.
The benchmark covers pure textual search and does not integrate non-textual relevance signals such as PageRank, recency, authority score, or click-through rate.

The annotation-bias analysis was carried out on a single dataset (TREC-COVID), and the missing judgements were annotated by the paper's authors, who were blind to which system retrieved each document.

Q10.text: The primary contribution is a heterogeneous, 18-dataset, 9-task zero-shot benchmark (BEIR) for evaluating IR model generalization.
A second contribution is a comparative zero-shot evaluation of 10 retrieval architectures, showing no single approach dominates and that in-domain performance does not predict generalization.
A third contribution is an analysis of annotation selection bias via manual TREC-COVID re-annotation, showing non-lexical approaches are disadvantaged by lexically biased annotation pools.
The authors released BEIR as a documented, extensible open-source package integrating diverse retrieval systems and datasets.

Q11.text: Long-document retrieval is not covered: most tasks have documents of at most a few hundred words, and the 512-word-piece limit of transformer models would require a different setup to compare approaches.
Multi-field retrieval is not covered: only datasets with one or two fields were included, although real collections can have many (title, abstract, body, authors, journal).
No error bars or repeated-run variance are reported, because most evaluated models are pre-trained checkpoints that the authors could not feasibly retrain.

Q12.text: BEIR is an 18-dataset, 9-task zero-shot benchmark showing that no single IR model architecture wins everywhere, and that in-domain accuracy does not predict out-of-domain generalization.
Re-ranking and late-interaction models generalize best but at the highest computational cost, while BM25 remains a strong zero-shot baseline.
Many BEIR datasets carry a lexical annotation bias that can understate the performance of non-lexical (e.g. dense) retrieval systems.
